Every morning, Sanad stood on the village wall, watching the young men train in the square at archery and horse riding.

What he wanted most was to be with them — and he was ten years old.

One day news came: a group of attackers was raiding the villages near the border, taking the sheep and burning the crops.

So the men and young men of the village got ready to go out to them and drive them away from the land.

Sanad ran to his father and said, "Take me with you, Father! I know how to shoot!"

His father stroked his head and said, "You are young, Sanad. War is for grown-ups."

So Sanad sat sadly by the door, watching the men prepare their swords while he had nothing to prepare.

Then Mays, the neighbors' daughter, who was memorizing Quran at the kuttab, came to him and said, "Why are you sad?"

He said, "They are all going out in the path of Allah except me."

She said, "Haven't you heard the hadith? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Whoever equips a fighter has fought, and whoever looks after a fighter's family well while he is away has fought.'"

Sanad said, "What does 'equip' mean?"

She said, "It means giving him what he needs for his journey. And looking after his family means taking care of what his family needs until he comes back."

Sanad got up from where he was sitting. Now he knew what to do.

Layth was the youngest of the young men going out, and the poorest. He had nothing but an old bow and a few arrows.

So Sanad went to his box, took out the coins he had saved, bought a bundle of arrows with them, and carried it to Layth.

Mays came with a bag of dates and dry bread that her mother had sewn, and said, "This is for your journey, Layth."

Layth took it and said, "May Allah reward you both with good. Your arrows will be with me, Sanad, and your food, Mays."

When the men had gone, Sanad went every morning to Umm Layth's house. He carried water for her from the well and took her sheep out to graze with his father's sheep.

And Mays brought her bread whenever her own mother baked.

After some days, the men came back to the village. They had driven the attackers away from the border.

Layth got off his horse, came to Sanad, took an arrow out of his quiver, and said, "This is the last arrow left of the ones you gave me. Keep it. You were with us, Sanad."

Sanad hung the arrow above his bed. He looked at it every night and knew that he had not just stayed at home.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever equips a fighter in the path of Allah has fought, and whoever looks after a fighter's family well in the path of Allah has fought."

📖 Agreed upon (Al-Bukhari and Muslim). This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.
